title: Look Back to Reason Forward: Revisitable Memory for Long-Context LLM Agents
claim: Retrieval-based and linear-overwrite memory approaches lose or bloat information; adding a callback to past memories enables non-linear access with light storage.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right, divided by vertical lines, dashed prompt boxes beneath
description: Three side-by-side panels separated by vertical lines, titled (a) Full-Text Context Retrieval, (b) Memorize while Reading, (c) Memorize with Callback. Panel (a) shows a pile of books feeding a retriever, which passes partial documents to an LLM that answers a question. Red crosses mark heavy storage burden and partial info. Panel (b) shows document chunks d1..dT, each feeding an LLM box that writes a memory note. Memory passes linearly from one step to the next, and the final LLM answers the question. Red crosses mark pruning of latent evidence and progressive information loss. Panel (c) has the same chunk-by-chunk flow, plus a green LLM-summarized key memory store that each LLM reads from and writes to. A retrieve-past-memory arrow feeds the last step. Green checkmarks mark non-linear visiting and light storage. Dashed boxes at the bottom of each panel give input/output prompt templates. Red and green text carries the contrast.
caption: \syr{ Comparison of memory paradigms. (a) Full-Text Retrieval separates retrieval from reasoning and incurs heavy storage burden. (b) "Memorize while Reading" paradigm suffers from progressive information loss and important information neglection due to linear memory overwriting. (c) This work introduces a callback mechanism, enabling non-linear memory visiting over past details and light-weighted storage. }
abstract: Large language models face challenges in long-context question answering, where key evidence of a query may be dispersed across millions of tokens. Existing works equip large language models with a memory buffer that is dynamically updated via a linear document scan, also known as the "memorize while reading" methods. While this approach scales efficiently, it suffers from pruning of latent evidence, information loss through overwriting, and sparse reinforcement learning signals. To tackle these challenges, we present ReMemR1, which integrates the mechanism of memory retrieval into the memory update process, enabling the agent to selectively callback historical memories for non-linear reasoning. To further strengthen training, we propose a multi-level reward design, which combines final-answer rewards with dense, step-level signals that guide effective memory use. Together, these contributions mitigate information degradation, improve supervision, and support complex multi-hop reasoning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ReMemR1 significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on long-context question answering while incurring negligible computational overhead, validating its ability to trade marginal cost for robust long-context reasoning.
